claims.text: As-synthesized HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure.
A GNN can be trained using combined microstructural images and mechanical-test data for HfNbTiVAl10.
Grain boundaries, phase distributions, and defect networks mediate the alloy's macroscopic mechanical response.
A GNN using self-attention and graph connectivity can capture multiscale interactions between microstructural features and mechanical responses.
Representing both local and global deformation mechanisms will improve the model's property predictions.
The proposed model will predict Young's modulus more accurately and rapidly than established multiscale simulations.
The proposed model will predict yield strength more accurately and rapidly than established multiscale simulations.
The proposed model will predict fracture-related behavior more accurately and rapidly than established multiscale simulations.
Traditional simulations have average prediction errors of approximately 20% to 30% for the target properties.
The proposed model could reduce average prediction error across the target properties to below 15%.
The proposed model could reduce computational time by approximately one order of magnitude.
High-fidelity atomistic and finite-element simulation methods are computationally intensive.
Established simulations are less able to decouple local microstructural effects from overall mechanical responses.
Prediction performance may fail to improve if the training data do not span the full range of microstructural variability.
Unreliable extraction or quantification of hierarchical features may cause significant prediction errors.
Extreme test conditions dominated by nonlinear deformation mechanisms may lie outside the model's predictive scope.
Variation in processing or environmental conditions may create additional scaling and generalization challenges.
The magnitude of the accuracy and efficiency gains cannot be established until a sufficiently large and diverse training dataset exists.
Independent samples tested under conditions identical to those simulated can be used to compare GNN predictions, established simulations, and measured properties.
An average error above 15%, or no statistically significant joint improvement in accuracy and computational efficiency, is declared to falsify the hypothesis.
